newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Computers about to turn Singapore law on its head.
newsitem.headline: Computers about to turn Singapore law on its head.

text.p: A personal computer and an Internet link could soon be all you need to get justice in Singapore after the country's top judge unveiled a hi-tech computer system for the courts.

This could ultimately allow virtual court hearings to be conducted from home. "It will...alter completely the manner in which advocates do legal research, draft and file papers and conduct trials in the courtroom," Chief Justice Yong Pung How said at the launch of the S$80.0 million (US$56.8 million) system on Saturday.
Yong described the system as "the judiciary's most ambitious technological project to date".

The judiciary expects administrative savings of S$4 million a year and a significant improvement in the speed of delivering justice as a result of the system, which is scheduled for full implementation by 2000.
The Electronic Filing System (EFS) will allow court documents to be filed remotely from a lawyer's office or home, and enable open court and chamber hearings to be conducted electronically.
For Singapore, keen to be seen as the hub of Information Technology innovation, bringing the virtual courtroom one step closer is evidently an image booster.
But the big question is whether Singapore's 600-odd law firms can make the leap from a centuries old profession steeped in tradition to the cutting edge of technology.
"The main concern of the legal community is that they may not have sufficient time to become accustomed to EFS," the Supreme Court said in a written response to queries.
"We're talking about change, and in legal circles that change is not always so fast," Randolph Khoo, a partner with one of Singapore's largest law firms, told Reuters.
And as for the virtual courtroom, Khoo said: "We're moving close to that, but at the moment we've got some serious evidential rules that need to be considered."
Evidence and exhibits must be physically presented at a trial. Until technology can overcome this, or the law is changed, the need for a courtroom remains, he said.
Cross-examination of witnesses was seen as a major difficulty by another lawyer, who declined to be identified.
"I really do appreciate the feel of a trial environment," he said. "One has to look at demeanour, how the witness presents himself, and that would risk being lost."
Cost is another factor putting some lawyers off. They estimate installing EFS would cost them S$30,000 to S$40,000.

Authorised EFS bureaux will provide filing services for firms without systems, but charges are 50 percent higher than current court fees. They would rise "to provide an incentive to law firms" to buy the system, the Supreme Court said.
Lawyers recognise that the technology train is unstoppable.
"I think we're pragmatic people," Khoo said. "Technology is the way of the future -- why should we be left behind?"
